paras: The whitecapping of John Baxter was a night attack at Smithfield, Pennsylvania, in August 1890, in which eight or ten masked men whipped Baxter, a Black man, with cowhides after he ignored a notice signed "White Caps" ordering him to leave the community. The notice had been sent to Baxter and Mrs. Jennie Smith, a white woman living with him, and she fled before the band arrived. White papers from Pennsylvania to Washington and Tennessee printed the Uniontown dispatch, one under the headline "White Caps Are Sometimes Right."

According to a dispatch dated Uniontown, Pa., August 16, Baxter, described as "colored," and Smith, described as white, had lately been living together at Smithfield. The same dispatch said, without naming a source, that the two had taken over the house of Baxter's "old father," driving him out and "compelling him to sleep in barns." The couple then received a notice signed "White Caps" warning them to quit the community or take the consequences. Baxter, who thought he knew who had written it, wrote "Come on. I dare you to come" on the back, signed it "Texas John," and mailed it to that man.

Smith heeded the warning and left, but Baxter stayed. Some time later a rap at the door woke him around midnight, and he found eight or ten masked men waiting, each with a cowhide. He fought back but was overpowered, and the dispatch called what followed "one of the most terrible beatings ever heard of in this community."
The reports name none of the attackers, and no report of an arrest or prosecution was found.

The story went out from Uniontown in two forms. A condensed version, which put the attackers at ten and the attack on "Last Monday night," ran on August 19 in the Washington Evening Star as "Cowhided by White Caps" and in the Clarksville Daily Tobacco Leaf-Chronicle as "White Caps Are Sometimes Right." The full text appeared in the Somerset Herald on August 20 and in the Evening Star on August 21, the latter headed "A Double Dose of Whipping" over the line "The Woman Having Fled, the White Caps Gave the Man Enough for Both."

The full dispatch called the couple "the guilty pair" and Baxter Smith's "paramour," described the attackers as "stalwart men," and told the father story as fact. Even so, both forms of the dispatch granted that Baxter "fought pluckily" before he was overpowered. The Cambria Freeman of Ebensburg gave the episode a single sentence among miscellaneous news on August 22, calling Smith the man's "white paramour." All of the coverage found came from white papers; no Black-press report was found.

The reports differ on the date: the condensed dispatch said "Last Monday night," the Cambria Freeman said "Friday night," and the full dispatch, dated August 16, gave no day. The Freeman also named the man "John Williams," said the couple had been warned to leave "Uniontown," and said the masked men "broke into his bedroom" rather than calling him to the door. Four printings of the Uniontown dispatch agree on the name Baxter and on Smithfield, and the Freeman's brief rewrite appears to have taken the dateline town for the place.

accounts.label: Uniontown dispatch, full version

accounts.label: Uniontown dispatch, condensed wire version
accounts.gist: The couple ignored a whitecap warning; 'Last Monday night' ten masked men with cowhides called Baxter to his door and beat him after he fought.

accounts.label: Cambria Freeman news note
accounts.gist: 'John Williams' and his 'white paramour' were warned to leave Uniontown; she went, he stayed, and 'Friday night' masked men broke into his bedroom and whipped him with rawhides.
